<div class="slide-content"><p>Generalized Fluid System Simulation Program (GFSSP)</p>
<p>4</p>
<div class="embedded" id="slide4_rId2"></div>
<p>System level CFD code developed at NASA in the early 90s </p>
<div class="embedded" id="slide4_rId3"></div>
<p>Fluid Nodes:  mass and energy equations are solved for pressures and enthalpies</p>
<p>Fluid Branches:  momentum equation is solved for flowrates</p>
<p>Fluid-to-Solid Conductors:  conjugate heat transfer</p>
<p>Solid Nodes:  solid energy equation is solved for wall temperature</p>
<p>Fluid Boundary Nodes</p>
<p>Solid-to-Solid Conductors</p>
<p>User subroutines are added for advanced physics</p>
<p>Fluid network  }</p>
<p>Solid network  }</p>

<div class="slide-content"><p>I.  Evaporation Mass Transfer Model</p>
<p>When pressurant (e.g., helium) is injected into the liquid (e.g., LOx), there exists a species concentration gradient:</p>
<p>LOx evaporates and diffuses into helium bubbles (quick process)</p>
<p>Helium (a non-condensable) dissolves into surrounding LOx (slow process)</p>
<p></p>
<p>		     :  Species flux [</p>
<p>	(analogous to Newton’s 	     :  Mass transfer coefficient [</p>
<p>	        Law of Cooling)	    :  Species concentration [</p>
<p></p>
<p>Analysis using the above equation is empirical, tedious, and uncertainty-prone; we have implemented an instantaneous heat and mass transfer model as an approximation (approach supported by literature)</p>
<p></p>
<div class="embedded" id="slide6_rId3"></div>
<p>Mass transfer equilibrium time scale on the order of hundredths of seconds</p>
<p>Heat transfer equilibrium time scale on the order of seconds to tens of seconds</p>
</div>
<div class="slide-master-content"></div>
<div class="slide-content"><p>I.  Evaporation Mass Transfer Model</p>
<p>Dalton’s Law of Partial Pressure:			(Equation 1)</p>
<p></p>
<p>Ideal Gas Equation of State:	He:	 </p>
<p>				GO2:	</p>
<p>						(Equation 2)</p>
<p></p>
<p>These equations are applied as the bubbles are entering the ullage, so </p>

<div class="slide-content"><p>II.  Dissolution Mass Transfer Model:  physics and assumptions</p>
<p>   (Newton’s Law of Cooling analogy)</p>
<p></p>
<p>  (per bubble)</p>
<p></p>
<p>Instantaneous heat and mass transfer assumption from the evaporation model still apply, but the mass transfer due to dissolution occurs at a slower time scale and must be tracked</p>
<p>  Dissolution is assumed to occur at a constant rate as the bubble rises</p>
<p>  Model assumes  at all times</p>
<div class="embedded" id="slide11_rId3"></div>
</div>
<div class="slide-master-content"></div>
<div class="slide-content"><p>II.  Dissolution Mass Transfer Model:  unknowns</p>
<p>  (per bubble)</p>
<p></p>
<p>  (Whitaker [3] correlation)</p>
<p>   		(Wilkes and Chang [4] correlation)</p>
<p> 				(Talaia [5])</p>
<p>Average initial bubble diameter was estimated to be the same as the hole sizes on the diffuser</p>

<div class="slide-content"><p>Conclusions</p>
<p>LOx/He submerged pressurization systems (w/o dissolution):</p>
<p>GFSSP can predict liquid subcooling to within 1.5 K for all cases simulated while varying injection flowrate, injection temperature, propellant drain rate, and ullage pressure parameters.  </p>
<p>Helium requirements are predicted to within 20% for all but one case.</p>
<p>H2/He submerged pressurization systems (w/ dissolution):</p>
<p>In the four CPST EDU cases simulated, maximum ullage pressure error is less than 10%</p>
<p>Unknown uncertainty in the two empirical correlations used in model</p>
<p>Size of injected helium bubbles is unknown and is currently being prescribed</p>
<p>Without more data, model is insufficient as a predictive tool but is shown to model available data well</p>
